name: Hotel-Dieu
short_description: Paris's oldest hospital, founded in the 12th century by Bishop Maurice de Sully, with a harrowing history of overcrowding.

beats.script_body: The Hotel-Dieu is the oldest hospital in Paris, founded in the 12th century by Maurice de Sully, the same bishop who initiated the construction of Notre-Dame. For centuries it was the only hospital serving the city, and conditions were appalling — up to five patients were crammed into a single bed.
physical_cues: Hotel-Dieu building on the Ile de la Cite
beats.source_passage: Oldest hospital, founded 12th century by Maurice de Sully, 5 patients per bed

beats.script_body: Contemporary accounts described the Hotel-Dieu's wards as containing 'the ill, the dying and the dead' sharing the same beds. Philippe-Auguste donated the straw from his royal horses to serve as bedding. The stench was so overwhelming that visitors could smell the hospital from across the river.
physical_cues: Hotel-Dieu entrance
beats.source_passage: The ill, the dying and the dead sharing beds; Philippe-Auguste offered horse straw

beats.script_body: The old Pont au Double, which connected the Hotel-Dieu to the Left Bank, featured an enclosed glass gallery where recovering patients could promenade — an early form of therapeutic architecture, allowing the sick to take the air without leaving the hospital.
physical_cues: Look toward the Pont au Double
beats.source_passage: Pont au Double glass gallery promenade for patients

opening_hours_basis: An active hospital with a public inner courtyard/chapel behind entrances; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Working hospital with a long facade on the Notre-Dame parvis and an inner courtyard glimpse; it is not a visitor interior, so priced outside only.
judgement_basis: A functioning hospital with a quiet interior courtyard where running and casual sitting are inappropriate, but it sits on the open, lit, well-populated Ile de la Cite near Notre-Dame after dark.
queue_basis: A working hospital, not a ticketed attraction; a tourist stops to look at the facade and courtyard from the street and never joins any admission line.

name: Notre-Dame Cathedral
short_description: Medieval cathedral on Ile de la Cite, one of the finest examples of French Gothic architecture

beats.script_body: During the Revolution, Notre-Dame was nearly lost forever. Stripped of its treasures and rededicated to the Cult of Reason, it was put up for sale as building material. A certain Citoyen Simon nearly purchased the cathedral — one of the closest brushes with destruction in the building's history.
physical_cues: Notre-Dame exterior
beats.source_passage: Nearly sold during Revolution; Citoyen Simon nearly bought it

beats.script_body: Eugene Viollet-le-Duc began his controversial restoration of Notre-Dame in 1844, guided by his famous principle: 'To restore a building is not to maintain it, repair it, or rebuild it; it is to re-establish it in a complete state which may never have existed at any given moment.' He added the spire, the gargoyles, and much of what the world came to think of as 'original' medieval decoration.
physical_cues: Look at the gargoyles and chimeras — most are Viollet-le-Duc additions
beats.source_passage: Viollet-le-Duc restoration from 1844; restoring does not mean maintaining

beats.script_body: Victor Hugo's 1831 novel The Hunchback of Notre-Dame was written partly as a plea to save the crumbling cathedral. The book ignited a wave of public passion for the medieval monument and directly led to the campaign for its restoration — proof that a novel can save a building.
physical_cues: Notre-Dame facade
beats.source_passage: Hugo's Hunchback saved the cathedral

beats.script_body: Notre-Dame endured centuries of vandalism before the Revolution even began. The medieval chancel screen was destroyed in 1699 to make way for a more fashionable baroque interior. The original stained glass windows — except for the three great rose windows — were ripped out and replaced with plain white glass to 'let in more light.'
physical_cues: Notice the three surviving rose windows — the only original stained glass
beats.source_passage: Centuries of vandalism; chancel screen destroyed 1699; stained glass replaced

beats.script_body: During the Paris Commune in May 1871, Communards attempted to burn Notre-Dame by piling chairs and furniture against the doors and setting them alight. Doctors and staff from the neighbouring Hotel-Dieu rushed across and extinguished the flames, saving the cathedral from destruction.
physical_cues: Notre-Dame west doors
Hotel-Dieu across the square
beats.source_passage: Commune nearly burned it May 1871; Hotel-Dieu doctors extinguished fire

beats.script_body: The 28 statues of the Kings of Judah on the west facade were torn down by Revolutionaries who mistook them for the Kings of France. The heads were discovered in 1977 during construction work near the Opera and are now displayed at the Musee de Cluny.
physical_cues: Look at the Gallery of Kings on the west facade — these are 19th-century replacements
beats.source_passage: 28 Kings of Judah statues; smashed by Revolutionaries who mistook them for Kings of France

beats.script_body: Notre-Dame's great bell, known today as Emmanuel, has a dramatic history. The original bell, called Jacqueline, was recast in 1680 and renamed Emmanuel. According to tradition, the ladies of the court threw their jewellery into the molten metal, which is said to give the bell its exceptionally pure tone.
physical_cues: South tower of Notre-Dame where Emmanuel hangs
beats.source_passage: Jacqueline recast as Emmanuel 1680; ladies' jewellery melted in
beats.fact_check_notes: Corrected — Jacqueline did not survive; it was recast as Emmanuel.

beats.script_body: Notre-Dame was the birthplace of polyphonic music in Europe. In the 12th and 13th centuries, the composers Leonin and Perotin developed the art of organum — music in multiple voices — at the cathedral's choir school. Their innovations laid the foundations for all Western harmony.
physical_cues: Notre-Dame choir
beats.source_passage: Leonin and Perotin founded polyphonic school 12th-13th century

opening_hours_basis: Gated cathedral you enter through doors; hours since the 2024 reopening not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: The west facade with its portals and towers, plus the parvis and views from around the Ile de la Cite, absorb 25 minutes; the interior nave, chancel, rose windows and side chapels take around 35 minutes plus an entry queue since reopening.
judgement_basis: A cathedral interior demands silence and stillness so children cannot run and normal conversation is discouraged, and the surrounding parvis is open paving without quiet free seating; the Ile de la Cite location is lit and trafficked with people about, so being left standing after dark is fine.
queue_basis: Since the post-fire reopening entry is managed through a controlled single access point with high demand, forming a substantial line to walk into a free cathedral that eases only at opening and near closing.

anchors.label: The west front
anchors.basis: The whole facade — rose window, gallery and the row of kings together — is only visible from well back: a person STANDS on the parvis paving, sixty to eighty metres out, near the kilometre-zero star, and walks backwards until it fits (W7.11, 11/11: 45 m put the listener under the tympanum, craning). Eighty metres covers the paving people actually stand on and still stops short of the apse.

anchors.label: Inside
anchors.basis: Under the roof: the nave runs about sixty metres east from the door to the choir; GPS is unreliable inside, so this chapter is offered on the screen and never starts itself.

anchors.label: The east end
anchors.basis: Square Jean-XXIII is the strip you STAND in to look back along the flying buttresses; the view needs the length of the garden, not its gate. Fifty-five metres covers the walk without reaching the parvis (W7.11 defect 16).

name: Rue Chanoinesse
short_description: Medieval street on Ile de la Cite where Abelard and Heloise's tragic love affair unfolded.

beats.script_body: In 1118, the brilliant philosopher Peter Abelard came to this street to tutor the young Heloise, niece of Canon Fulbert. Their passionate love affair — one of the most famous in history — ended in catastrophe when Fulbert, enraged by a secret marriage and pregnancy, hired thugs to castrate Abelard. Heloise became a nun, Abelard a monk, and their anguished love letters became classics of medieval literature.
physical_cues: Walk along rue Chanoinesse and imagine the medieval cloister houses
beats.source_passage: Abelard and Heloise 1118; Canon Fulbert; castration

beats.script_body: The remains of Abelard and Heloise have had an extraordinary journey through the centuries. They were reunited in death and now lie together at Pere Lachaise cemetery — the most visited grave in that famous necropolis. Medallion portraits of the lovers can be seen at 9 quai aux Fleurs, near the site of their fateful encounter.
physical_cues: Look for medallions at 9 quai aux Fleurs
beats.source_passage: Lovers' remains journey; Pere Lachaise; medallions at 9 quai aux Fleurs

beats.script_body: The mathematician and philosopher Jean le Rond d'Alembert was found as a newborn on the steps of the church of Saint-Jean-le-Rond — which once stood near here — on 16 November 1717. A foundling abandoned by his mother, he was raised by a glazier's wife and went on to co-edit the Encyclopedie with Diderot, becoming one of the towering intellects of the Enlightenment.
physical_cues: The church of Saint-Jean-le-Rond no longer exists but stood near the north side of Notre-Dame
beats.source_passage: d'Alembert foundling at Saint-Jean-le-Rond, 16 Nov 1717

opening_hours_basis: A public medieval street walked freely at any hour, so not gated.
visit_basis: Medieval street on Ile de la Cite with old canons' houses to walk along slowly and look into; a street whose value is entirely outside, nothing to enter.
judgement_basis: A narrow medieval street on Ile de la Cite carrying occasional vehicles with no free seating and little quiet, and it is a deserted lane after dark rather than a lit populated place to leave someone standing.
queue_basis: An open medieval street with no interior and no gate, so nothing is ever queued for.

name: Memorial des Martyrs de la Deportation
short_description: Underground memorial at the tip of Ile de la Cite honouring the 200,000 deported from France during WWII.

beats.script_body: At the eastern tip of the Ile de la Cite, steps descend into a stark underground crypt — the Memorial des Martyrs de la Deportation. The narrow entrance forces visitors into single file, evoking the claustrophobia of deportation. The poet Robert Desnos, who had been active in the Resistance, died at the Theresienstadt concentration camp just weeks before liberation.
physical_cues: Descend the narrow steps at the tip of the island
The crypt with its 200,000 crystals of light
beats.source_passage: Crypt at tip of Ile de la Cite; Desnos died at Theresienstadt

opening_hours_basis: Door; hours are the place's own OpenStreetMap tag: Oct-Mar Tu-Su 10:00-17:00; Apr-Sep Tu-Su 10:00-19:00.
visit_basis: Stark underground memorial at the tip of Île de la Cité; you approach across the small garden above, then descend into the narrow crypt of 200,000 lights and inscriptions, a contemplative space taking about twenty minutes inside.
judgement_basis: This is a stark, silent underground memorial where running and casual conversation are socially unacceptable and there is no free open seating, and the site is closed and gated after dark.
queue_basis: The memorial is free but entered by a narrow staircase that admits only a few visitors at once, so a small line can form at midday while it is otherwise walk-straight-in.

name: Ile Saint-Louis
short_description: A tranquil island of 17th-century classical mansions east of Ile de la Cite

beats.script_body: The Ile Saint-Louis was developed in the first half of the 17th century, transforming two muddy islands — l'Ile Notre-Dame and l'Ile aux Vaches — into the elegant residential quarter you see today. Corneille marvelled at how 'a whole city had sprung from an old ditch.'
physical_cues: Walk along the quais and admire the 17th-century facades
beats.source_passage: 17th-century development; Corneille quote about city springing from old ditch

beats.script_body: The Hotel de Bretonvilliers, once the most splendid mansion on the island, was destroyed — a casualty of the same forces of modernisation and neglect that threatened the entire Marais before its 20th-century rehabilitation.
physical_cues: Eastern tip of Ile Saint-Louis where the mansion once stood
beats.source_passage: Hotel de Bretonvilliers, most splendid mansion, destroyed

beats.script_body: Marie Curie lived at 36 quai de Bethune from 1912 to 1934. Nearby, the cosmetics magnate Helena Rubinstein purchased a Le Vau mansion in 1932 — and to the horror of preservationists, demolished it in 1935 to build a modernist replacement.
physical_cues: Look for 36 quai de Bethune
beats.source_passage: Marie Curie at 36 quai de Bethune 1912-1934; Rubinstein demolished Le Vau mansion
beats.fact_check_notes: Rubinstein purchase 1932 not earlier date; demolition 1935.

beats.script_body: The restaurant Nos Ancetres les Gaulois on the island offers a distinctive dining experience — a ribald celebration of Gallic excess with unlimited wine and rustic fare, echoing the spirit of the Gauls who once inhabited this stretch of the Seine.
physical_cues: Look for the restaurant on rue Saint-Louis-en-l'Ile
beats.source_passage: Nos Ancetres les Gaulois restaurant

beats.script_body: The quai des Balcons earned its name from the series of ornate iron balconies lining its facades. The 18th-century writer Mercier observed that the island had 'its own moral code, its own customs' — a village within Paris that to this day retains an insular, self-contained atmosphere quite unlike the rest of the city.
physical_cues: Look at the iron balconies along the quai
beats.source_passage: Quai des Balcons; Mercier quote about island's moral code

opening_hours_basis: A residential Seine island of open streets and quays freely accessible from the street at any hour.
visit_basis: Small residential island with one main street of 17th-century townhouses, quays and an ice cream stop; the value is walking it, nothing single to enter.
judgement_basis: A residential island whose narrow streets carry cars and whose quays edge straight onto the Seine, so running children are at risk, but its tree-lined quay steps and benches are quiet enough to talk and the streets stay lit and inhabited at night.
queue_basis: A residential island of open streets and shopfronts with no controlled entrance, so nothing is queued before you walk onto it.

name: Berthillon
short_description: Legendary Parisian ice cream shop on Ile Saint-Louis, famous for its artisanal sorbets and glaces.

beats.script_body: Berthillon has been serving what many consider the finest ice cream in Paris from its shop at the western tip of the Ile Saint-Louis, with Notre-Dame Cathedral as its backdrop. The queues that snake along rue Saint-Louis-en-l'Ile are a Parisian institution in their own right.
physical_cues: Look for the queue — it's part of the experience
View of Notre-Dame from the tip of the island
beats.source_passage: Ice cream at western tip of island facing Notre-Dame

opening_hours_basis: An ice cream parlour entered through a door (gated); the flagship's published pattern is Wednesday-Sunday, closed Monday and Tuesday.
visit_basis: Famous ice cream parlour on Ile Saint-Louis; a few minutes at the corner shopfront, and inside a small salon or counter with a reliably long queue, so 15 min including waiting and choosing.
judgement_basis: A small ice cream shop on the narrow streets of Ile Saint-Louis with no free seating and shopfronts at child height; it closes in the evening and the quiet residential island offers little activity once shut.
queue_basis: A small ice-cream counter whose line is limited by one serving window, so afternoon and warm-season crowds form a real but bounded queue that shrinks to a few people off-peak; no security or ticket.

name: Pont-Marie
short_description: 17th-century stone bridge connecting the Ile Saint-Louis to the Right Bank, named after developer Christophe Marie.

beats.script_body: The Pont-Marie is named not for the Virgin Mary or Marie de Medici, as many assume, but for Christophe Marie, the entrepreneur who developed the Ile Saint-Louis in the 17th century. A statue of Sainte Genevieve, patroness of Paris, watches over the bridge.
physical_cues: Look for the Genevieve statue
Pont-Marie stonework
beats.source_passage: Named for Christophe Marie not Marie de Medici; Genevieve statue

opening_hours_basis: An open stone bridge crossed freely from the pavement, whole value in the open, so not gated.
visit_basis: 17th-century stone bridge you cross and pause on for river and island views; a destination in itself but with nothing to enter.
judgement_basis: A stone road bridge with traffic and low parapets onto the Seine offering no safe running room and no quiet free seating, but it is lit, open and crossed at all hours.
queue_basis: A stone bridge with no door and no ticket: you simply walk across it in the open, so there is no line.

name: Hotel de Lauzun
short_description: Opulent 17th-century mansion where Baudelaire lived and the Club des Haschichins gathered.

beats.script_body: Charles Baudelaire lived in a small apartment at the Hotel de Lauzun from 1843, where he began composing Les Fleurs du Mal. Theophile Gautier founded the Club des Haschichins here, and the literary elite gathered to experiment with hashish — evenings that Baudelaire later chronicled in his Artificial Paradises.
physical_cues: Hotel de Lauzun facade on quai d'Anjou
Baudelaire's top-floor windows
beats.source_passage: Baudelaire, Gautier, Club des Haschichins, Les Fleurs du Mal
beats.fact_check_notes: Date corrected — 1840 impossible; Baudelaire moved in 1843.

beats.script_body: The Hotel de Lauzun was built by architect Charles Chamois and features some of the most lavishly decorated interiors in Paris. The Duc de Lauzun, who gave the mansion its name, led a turbulent life — he secretly married the Grande Mademoiselle (Louis XIV's cousin) and was imprisoned in the fortress of Pignerol for his audacity.
physical_cues: Look at the ornate ironwork balcony
Hotel de Lauzun entrance
beats.source_passage: Duc de Lauzun's opulent interior; Pignerol fortress
beats.fact_check_notes: Architect corrected from Le Vau to Charles Chamois; Vignerol corrected to Pignerol.

opening_hours_basis: Marked walk-by only; a private mansion appreciated from the street facade, so not gated.
visit_basis: Opulent riverside mansion seen from the quay, its facade and ironwork the whole of the stop; interior is by rare special arrangement only, so not a normal entry.
judgement_basis: A closed private mansion on Ile Saint-Louis seen only from the narrow quay-side pavement with no free seating, though the riverside street is lit and moderately used at night.
queue_basis: A walk-by private mansion closed to the general public except rare special events, so no ticket line exists on an ordinary day.

name: Hotel Lambert
short_description: Le Vau's masterpiece on the Ile Saint-Louis, with a famous rotunda balcony and Polish exile heritage.

beats.script_body: The Hotel Lambert is considered Louis Le Vau's masterpiece of domestic architecture. Built for Lambert de Thorigny, it features a celebrated rotunda balcony that projects over the Seine. Prince Adam Czartoryski purchased it in 1843 and the Rothschild family acquired it in 1975.
physical_cues: Look for the rotunda balcony projecting over the water
Hotel Lambert on the quai d'Anjou
beats.source_passage: Le Vau masterpiece; rotunda balcony; Lambert de Thorigny
beats.fact_check_notes: Czartoryski purchase corrected from 1842 to 1843; Rothschilds corrected from 1976 to 1975.

beats.script_body: When Prince Czartoryski bought the Hotel Lambert, it became the centre of Polish exile in Paris. Chopin performed in its salons, and the poet Adam Mickiewicz was a frequent guest. A museum of Polish history was established here, preserving the memory of a nation that had lost its independence.
physical_cues: Hotel Lambert exterior
beats.source_passage: Czartoryski Polish exile; Chopin; Mickiewicz museum

opening_hours_basis: A private mansion behind gates not generally open to visitors; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Le Vau mansion at the tip of Ile Saint-Louis, its rotunda balcony and river-facing walls viewed from the quay and street corner; private residence, no public interior.
judgement_basis: A private mansion at the tip of Ile Saint-Louis viewed from a narrow pavement with river parapets nearby and no free seating, but the quay is lit and central for standing after dark.
queue_basis: A private residence viewed only from the street; with no public admission there is no queue to price.

name: Quai de Bourbon
short_description: Northern quay of the Ile Saint-Louis, home to sculptor Camille Claudel and poet Guillaume Apollinaire.

beats.script_body: The sculptor Camille Claudel had her studio on the quai de Bourbon from 1899 to 1913. These were her final years of creative freedom before she was committed to a psychiatric institution by her family, where she remained for the last thirty years of her life — one of the most tragic stories in the history of art.
physical_cues: Look along the quai for Claudel's former studio
beats.source_passage: Camille Claudel studio 1899-1913; tragically interned

beats.script_body: Guillaume Apollinaire lived at 43 quai de Bourbon, where he and the painter Marie Laurencin carried on their celebrated love affair. The building was known as the Maison du Centaure — a fitting address for the poet who championed Cubism and coined the term 'surrealism.'
physical_cues: Look for number 43 quai de Bourbon
beats.source_passage: Apollinaire at 43 quai de Bourbon; Marie Laurencin; Maison du Centaure

opening_hours_basis: An open riverside quay walked freely from the pavement, so not gated.
visit_basis: Northern quay of Ile Saint-Louis to stroll for river views and old house frontages; an outdoor walk with nothing to enter.
judgement_basis: A riverside quay on Ile Saint-Louis with road traffic and stone parapets onto the Seine, no reliable quiet free seating, and quiet dim conditions after dark on this residential island.
queue_basis: An open riverside quay with no door and no ticket; the whole experience is outdoors, so no line forms.

name: Crypte Archeologique de l'Ile de la Cite
short_description: Underground archaeological museum beneath the parvis of Notre-Dame, revealing ancient Lutetia.

beats.script_body: Beneath the parvis of Notre-Dame lies an underground museum revealing the layers of Paris's past. The archaeological crypt displays remains of ancient Lutetia — Gallo-Roman walls, a quay, a hypocaust heating system, and medieval cellars — two thousand years of history directly beneath your feet.
physical_cues: Look for the entrance on the parvis of Notre-Dame
Descend to see the Roman ruins below
beats.source_passage: Underground museum beneath Parvis Notre-Dame; ancient Lutetia

opening_hours_basis: An underground museum behind a ticket line; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Small parvis entrance, then an underground museum of excavated Roman and medieval foundations with walkways and displays, typical visit 35-40 min plus a short ticket queue.
judgement_basis: An enclosed underground museum where quiet is expected, with no free social seating, that is locked and inaccessible at night.
queue_basis: A small municipal museum with a single ticket desk at the entrance; a modest queue can build midday when Notre-Dame crowds spill in, but it stays minor and moves quickly.

name: Saint-Louis-en-l'Ile Church
short_description: Baroque church on Ile Saint-Louis designed by Le Vau, with a distinctive openwork iron spire.

beats.script_body: The church of Saint-Louis-en-l'Ile was designed by Louis Le Vau, the same architect who created the Hotel Lambert just down the street. Its most distinctive feature is the unusual openwork iron spire, quite unlike any other church tower in Paris. The nearby Hotel du Jeu de Paume recalls the island's quieter days.
physical_cues: Look up at the unusual openwork iron spire
Compare Le Vau's style here with the Hotel Lambert nearby
beats.source_passage: Le Vau design; unique openwork spire; Jeu de Paume hotel nearby

opening_hours_basis: A church one enters through a door; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Baroque church with an openwork spire seen from the street and a richly gilded single-nave interior, typical visit around 18 min.
judgement_basis: A quiet baroque church interior where running and casual conversation are out of place, fronting a narrow Ile Saint-Louis street that is dim and largely deserted once shops close at night.
queue_basis: A parish church with free open-door entry and no security screening, so visitors walk in directly without waiting in line.
